title: Complex chronic care management billed for 257 patients a month
what_we_see: In October 2026 the practice billed the complex care-management code (99487) for 257 patients, 213 of them with the add-on code (99489), all under the physician. That is 79% of the patients seen that month. The codes assert 21,810 minutes, about 364 hours, of the practice's own clinical staff time in one month. Nationally the complex code is about 8% of care-management claims, and at this pace the practice would bill roughly 0.5% of all complex care management Medicare paid in the country in 2024. Service dates are batched at month end. Only 42% of lines have been paid since June. In CMS public data the practice billed 1,300 to 2,000 of these a year from 2019 to 2022 and none in 2024. Care management is also the service with the highest error rate Medicare measures: 65% of standard care-management claims reviewed nationally in 2025 were improper. It is on the Florida Medicare contractor's list of active targeted reviews, and in April 2026 a Florida physician and practice were excluded from Medicare for five years over care-management claims not rendered.
rule: Each claim requires: two or more serious chronic conditions; the patient's consent recorded before the first claim; a comprehensive care plan; at least 60 minutes that month of clinical staff time directed by the billing practitioner (30 more for each add-on); and medical decisions of moderate or high complexity by that practitioner. Staff must be the practice's own or under contract to it. Time by a facility's nurses does not count. Only one practitioner may bill per patient per month. The service may be billed for residents of nursing and assisted living facilities.
exposure: The whole revenue line, at most about $160,000 a year at current volume and payment rates, plus repayment of amounts already paid if records do not support them, going back up to six years. Volume this far from the norm is what Medicare's program-integrity contractors screen for. A buyer would exclude this revenue unless it is documented.
recommended_review: Before the next monthly batch: pull 30 patient-months at random. For each, find the consent with its date, the care plan, a time log showing who did what on which day and for how long, and the physician's decision making. Add up the minutes logged for a month and compare with the hours the practice's staff actually had. If the records do not support 60 minutes, stop billing the complex code and have the attorney direct a review of past claims.
control: Bill care management only from a time log, at the code the logged minutes support (standard care management needs 20 minutes). Each month compare total minutes billed with staff hours available. Record consent as a required field. Set the place of service from the resident's status. Block claims for any patient who died, was discharged, or elected hospice during the month.

title: Visit levels far above national patterns in the hospital and nursing facilities
what_we_see: Subsequent hospital visits were billed at the top level (99233) 73.7% of the time, against 37.2% nationally. Every initial hospital visit was the top level (99223), against 59.5%. Subsequent nursing facility visits were the second-highest level (99309) 95.6% of the time, against 48.8%, and every initial nursing facility visit was the top level (99306), against 48.5%. Both discharge-day families were billed only at the longer code. In CMS data the physician's top-level share of hospital follow-up visits was 64.5% in 2023, 1.3% in 2024 and is 73.7% now. As billed, the physician's work units run near three times the family medicine median. Visit frequency itself looks ordinary: 218 visits to 135 nursing facility residents in October, 1.6 each, with 14 residents seen four or more times.
rule: The level of a visit must follow the complexity of medical decision making, or total time, that the note documents for that day, and the service must be medically necessary. A sick population can justify a high average. It does not justify the same level on nearly every visit.
exposure: The difference between adjacent levels is roughly $20 to $45 a visit. On about 6,000 visits a year, a finding that half were one level high would be on the order of $60,000 to $100,000 a year, and Medicare contractors extrapolate from samples. Nationally, 25.5% of claims for the top initial nursing facility code, which this practice bills on every admission, were improper in Medicare's 2025 review. In July 2026 the Inspector General reported that 42 of 60 sampled nursing home visits failed review, and a nationwide audit of these services opened in April 2026.
recommended_review: Through the attorney, hire an independent certified auditor to review 10 notes per code family for each clinician, about 60 to 80 notes, chosen at random from the last six months. Ask for under-coding as well as over-coding. Decide next steps from the result.
control: Quarterly audit of 10 charts per clinician. A monthly table of each clinician's level mix against the national mix. Coding education built from the audit's findings. Levels chosen by the clinician in the note, never changed downstream.

title: Every nursing facility visit billed as a Medicare Part A skilled stay
what_we_see: All nursing facility visits and 152 of October's care-management lines carry place of service 31, the code for a patient in a Medicare Part A covered skilled stay. Place of service 32, for residents who are not in such a stay, was never used. With five facilities and many long-term residents, a large share of these claims almost certainly name the wrong setting.
rule: Medicare's manual says to use place of service 31 when the patient is in a Part A skilled stay and 32 when the patient is not, even in the same building. The setting changes the payment rate: 31 pays the facility rate and 32 the non-facility rate.
exposure: For visit codes the two rates have been close, so the dollars per claim are small either way, but the claims are inaccurate. For care management the facility rate is about a third lower, so long-term residents billed as 31 are underpaid. The 2026 and 2027 Medicare rules widen the gap between settings. Wrong setting codes also undermine the practice's credibility in any audit.
recommended_review: Ask each facility for a current census showing which residents are in a Part A skilled stay. Compare with the last three months of claims and count how many carried the wrong code and the payment difference in each direction.
control: A weekly census from every facility with skilled-stay status and payer, stored with the patient, from which the billing routine sets place of service for each date of service.

title: Initial nursing facility visits billed by the nurse practitioner in skilled stays
what_we_see: The nurse practitioner billed 10 of the 19 initial nursing facility visits in the charge feed, all at the top level and all as skilled stays. CMS data show she billed that code 37 times in 2023 and 129 times in 2024.
rule: A nurse practitioner may bill an initial nursing facility code for a medically necessary first evaluation. But in a skilled nursing facility the physician must personally perform the federally required initial comprehensive visit, no later than 30 days after admission, and may not delegate it. After that visit, alternate required visits may be delegated.
exposure: If the nurse practitioner's visit was the only comprehensive visit, the facility is out of compliance with its survey rules and the practice's claim misdescribes who performed a required physician task. Facilities are cited for this, and it can cost a medical directorship or the relationship.
recommended_review: For each skilled admission in the last six months where the nurse practitioner did the first visit, find the date and note of the physician's own comprehensive visit.
control: Track, for every skilled admission, the due date and the completion date of the physician's comprehensive visit, and the 30-day and 60-day visits that follow.

title: No coding audit and no compliance program on record
what_we_see: The practice has written billing rules and runs the monthly exclusion check. Nothing else of a compliance program is evidenced: no named compliance contact, no training record, no audit, no log of problems found and fixed. Billing is run by software agents under standing rules that include automatic write-offs and re-dating denied care-management claims.
rule: A compliance program is voluntary for a small practice, but federal guidance describes seven elements and treats a working program as evidence of good faith. The duty to return overpayments is not voluntary, and since 2025 it is triggered when a practice knew or should have known.
exposure: Without a program the practice cannot show that an error was an honest mistake caught by its own controls. That difference decides whether a problem ends in a refund or in penalties.
recommended_review: With the attorney, write a short program sized to two clinicians. Start with the audit, because its results decide everything else.
control: A named compliance contact, an annual training hour, a quarterly chart audit, a log of issues and corrections, and a yearly review of the billing rulebook by the auditor.

title: Possible overpayments with a legal deadline once identified
what_we_see: Four patterns in this review could each mean Medicare paid more than the records support: complex care management, visit levels, place of service, and initial visits. None has been tested against charts.
rule: A provider must report and return an overpayment within 60 days of identifying it. Identification includes what the provider should have known. A timely, good-faith investigation can suspend the deadline for up to 180 days. The lookback is six years.
exposure: Money kept after the deadline can become a false claim: three times the amount plus a penalty of $14,308 to $28,619 for each claim at current levels. Acting promptly and on advice keeps a billing problem a refund.
recommended_review: Have the attorney open and direct the review so that it is privileged, record the start date, and set the sample plan with the auditor.
control: A standing rule: any audit finding of an overpayment goes to the attorney the same week, with a dated record of what was decided.

title: Medical director payments from facilities that refer patients
what_we_see: Two nursing facilities pay the practice a medical director stipend, $12,000 each in the first nine months of 2026, and the practice also treats and bills for those facilities' residents. Whether written agreements, fair-market-value support and time records exist has not been confirmed.
rule: Payments between a physician and an entity that refers patients must fit an exception: a signed written agreement of at least a year, pay set in advance at fair market value, not tied to the volume or value of referrals, and for services actually performed and documented.
exposure: An arrangement that fails the exception taints the claims connected to it. Regulators have specifically warned about medical director agreements with little documented work.
recommended_review: Collect both agreements and twelve months of time logs. Have the attorney confirm each fits the personal services exception and safe harbor.
control: A monthly time log for each directorship, signed by the physician and sent to the facility, and a calendar reminder 90 days before each agreement ends.

title: Enrollment and credentialing gaps, with a Medicaid deadline on December 1
what_we_see: At least nine enrollment problems are open. The physician's Florida Medicaid provider agreement renewal is due December 1, 2026 and the nurse practitioner's revalidation was returned incomplete. A commercial plan terminated the practice after a missed recredentialing. Railroad Medicare claims are being written off because the practice is not enrolled. The nurse practitioner's national provider record is out of date.
rule: A claim is payable only if the clinician was enrolled with that payer on the date of service. Medicaid enrollment is also what allows secondary payment on dual-eligible patients, who are about four in ten of the practice's Medicare patients.
exposure: Lost secondary payments and denied claims until fixed, and services that can never be billed for the gap period. 108 denied visits are already tagged credentialing.
recommended_review: File the Medicaid renewal this week and confirm receipt. Then rank the remaining items by dollars affected.
control: One calendar of every enrollment, license and registration expiry for both clinicians with 90-day warnings, checked at the monthly review.

title: The practice depends on one physician and a few sites
what_we_see: The owner bills 76.8% of charges, holds the facility and hospital relationships, manages the finances and maintains the billing rulebook. One hospital is 37.8% of charges and the top three sites are 64.8%. Medical director stipends have fallen from $185,300 in 2023 to about $32,000 a year.
rule: This is a business risk, not a rule. Insurers, lenders and buyers all ask the same question: what happens to revenue if the owner is out, or if the largest site changes its physician coverage.
exposure: An illness, a change of hospital administration or the loss of one facility could remove a third or more of revenue within weeks. The same dependence is the main reason a buyer would discount the price.
recommended_review: Write down what would happen in each case and what it would cost.
control: A covering physician under written agreement, a second clinician known at every site, disability and key-person insurance, and written agreements with the main facilities.

title: Software agents act on billing rules that have not been independently reviewed
what_we_see: Agents enter charges, send claims, post payments, re-send denied claims and write off old balances every few hours under a written rulebook. Rules include writing off balances over a year old ($40,686 on November 2, 2026) and re-dating a care-management claim to month end after a frequency denial. This application also allows anyone to create a sign-in, although only approved addresses can see data.
rule: The practice is responsible for every claim submitted in its name, whoever or whatever prepares it. Under the False Claims Act, knowing includes reckless disregard, with no proof of intent needed. Florida's Medicaid law gives the provider an affirmative duty to supervise the preparation and submission of claims. Changing a code, date, modifier or diagnosis after a denial is acceptable only when the record supports the change and a qualified person has checked it. Routine write-off of what patients owe is also unlawful, so write-offs need a reason code.
exposure: An automated rule that is wrong is wrong on every claim it touches, and it leaves a complete log of having done so. In 2025 a physician group paid $45 million over allegations that its billing software was set to bill the higher-paid service every time.
recommended_review: Have the coding auditor read every rule that changes a code, date, modifier, diagnosis, place of service or balance. Sample 25 automated actions against the charts. Confirm that the automatic write-off rule touches insurance balances only and records a reason.
control: Human approval for any rule that changes a claim's code, date or place of service. A monthly sample of automated actions. Open sign-up turned off and access keys rotated.

title: Unknown status in Medicare's quality payment program
what_we_see: Neither clinician's status in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System is known. In 2024 Medicare paid the two clinicians about $350,000, well above the low-volume exclusion.
rule: Eligible clinicians who do not report receive the maximum negative adjustment, 9% of Medicare Part B payments, two years after the performance year. Small practices have simpler reporting options and can apply for hardship exceptions.
recommended_review: Look up both clinicians in the participation status tool, read the latest performance feedback, and note the reporting deadline for the 2026 performance year.
control: A calendar entry each January to confirm status and each March to submit.

title: Thin cash and expensive debt against an audit or a lost site
what_we_see: Cash covers about 48 days of spending. The main loan costs 13.99%. The owner drew $311,241 in salary and distributions in nine months and owes the corporation $162,121.
rule: Not a rule. Medicare can suspend payments or require repayment during an audit, and it is 55.5% of charges.
exposure: A payment hold or a refund demand of even $100,000 would exceed the cash on hand.
recommended_review: With the accountant, set a cash floor and a plan for the loan and the amount owed by the owner.
control: A 13-week cash forecast, a 90-day cash floor before distributions, and an unused line of credit.

title: Advance care planning billed without a tested record of time and consent
what_we_see: Advance care planning (99497) was billed on 62 encounters in the charge feed, about 8% of face-to-face visits, usually on the same day as an admission or another visit. In CMS data the two clinicians billed it about 650 to 880 times a year from 2019 to 2024. Whether each note records the time and who took part has not been checked.
rule: The conversation must be voluntary, and the note should say so, name who was present, and state the minutes. The first code needs at least 16 minutes. Billing it again for the same patient needs a documented change in health or wishes. Time counted here cannot also count toward the visit billed the same day. From January 1, 2027, planning done by staff uses separate codes.
exposure: Nationally 29.8% of these claims were improper in Medicare's 2025 review, nine in ten for insufficient documentation. At about $70 each and several hundred a year, the dollars are modest, but it is an easy finding for a reviewer.
recommended_review: Include 10 advance care planning notes in the outside audit.
control: A note template that will not release the code without minutes, participants and a statement that the discussion was voluntary.
